{{Short description|Theorem in Euclidean geometry}}
{{other uses|Carnot's theorem (disambiguation)}}
[[Image:Carnot theorem2.svg|345px|right|thumb|<math>|DG| + |DH| - |DF| = R + r </math>]]

In [[Euclidean geometry]], '''Carnot's theorem''' ({{IPAc-en|lang|k|ɑːr|ˈ|n|oʊ}} {{respell|kar|NOH}}, {{IPA|fr|kaʁno|lang}}) states that the sum of the [[signed distance]]s from the [[circumcenter]] <math>D</math> to the sides of an arbitrary triangle <math>ABC</math> is
<math display=block>DF + DG + DH = R + r,\ </math>

where <math>r</math> is the [[inradius]] and <math>R</math> is the [[circumradius]] of the triangle. Here the sign of the [[distances]] is taken to be negative if and only if the open [[line segment]] <math>DX</math> (for <math>X</math> equal to <math>F</math>, <math>G</math>, or <math>H</math>) lies completely outside the triangle. For example, in the diagram, <math>DF</math> is negative and both <math>DG</math> and <math>DH</math> are positive. The theorem can be viewed as saying that the sum of the actual-distance [[trilinear coordinates]] of the circumcenter is <math>R+r</math>.

The theorem is named after [[Lazare Carnot]] (1753&ndash;1823). It is used in a proof of the [[Japanese theorem for concyclic polygons]].
